headline: Mostly dry and a bit cooler than normal with light rain chances Sunday into Monday and again midweek, but the big story is a serious risk of moderate to major coastal flooding during Thanksgiving week.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: A weak disturbance passing Friday evening brings only scattered light showers north of Point Conception, with a few hundredths of an inch at most; the Glendale and Los Angeles areas stay dry. Light northeast winds develop tonight into Saturday morning in the usual wind-prone spots, but speeds stay below advisory levels. Overnight lows are chilly, with some areas dropping below freezing.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Saturday is dry, and the light winds off the land warm things up a bit, mainly west of the mountains, with highs in the mid to upper 60s; temperatures generally run about 5 degrees below normal. A weak storm brings a decent chance of measurable rain from Sunday (mainly Sunday night) into Monday morning, with totals of a quarter inch or less and no flooding concerns. Highs vary only a little from day to day Sunday and Monday.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Another storm crosses the area Tuesday night through Wednesday night, though it does not look very strong. Los Angeles and Ventura counties have lower chances of measurable rain, with around a tenth of an inch or less if any falls, while San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties will likely see 0.10–0.50 inch, more near Rocky Butte. Thanksgiving Day and Friday look dry as high pressure builds and light winds blow off the land, with highs in the mid 60s to mid 70s.

coast: Forecasters have significant concern for moderate to major coastal flooding Thanksgiving week, as unusually high sea levels from warm ocean water, extra-high spring tides and a large, long-period west swell combine. For the Central Coast, Ventura and Los Angeles coasts, a Coastal Flood Advisory runs from 3 AM Monday to 3 AM Wednesday (shallow flooding of beach parking lots and low roads, moderate beach erosion), followed by a Coastal Flood Watch from late Tuesday night through Thursday afternoon, when the swell arrives and significant impacts seem probable. Peak high tides come between about 8:45 and 10 AM, around 8.2–8.6 feet for LA and Ventura and 7.9–8.2 feet on the Central Coast, with a reasonable worst case 0.3–0.5 foot higher; if upgraded to a warning, flooding could reach farther inland and damage coastal roads and buildings. Areas of greatest concern include Santa Monica to Palos Verdes and Long Beach/Naples in LA County; Faria to Silver Strand Beach, inside harbors and Ventura Harbor in Ventura County; and Morro Bay, Pismo Beach, Oceano Dunes and the Cayucos, Avila and Pismo piers. The Santa Barbara South Coast (Santa Barbara to Rincon, plus Jalama Beach) and Catalina and the Channel Islands are under a Coastal Flood Advisory from 3 AM Monday to 3 PM Thursday, with elevated to high surf likely all week and more alerts likely for Friday. Officials advise heeding local authorities, protecting flood-prone property with sandbags or barriers, and staying off rock jetties and flooded roads and walkways. Offshore, Small Craft Advisories continue until 9 PM tonight or 3 AM Saturday depending on the zone, conditions turn fairly mild Saturday, a weak front Sunday into Monday has minimal impact, and a stronger cold front Tuesday night into Wednesday brings wind and rain mainly off the Central Coast, with small-craft-level northwest winds possible south of Point Conception Wednesday and Wednesday night and large seas returning mid to late week.
watch_for: Coastal flooding Wednesday–Thursday: the watch could be upgraded to a Coastal Flood Warning as the big swell meets peak morning high tides around 8.2–8.6 feet in LA and Ventura.
Light rain Sunday into Monday morning, a quarter inch or less.
The Tuesday night–Wednesday night storm: likely light rain on the Central Coast, less certain and lighter (0.10 inch or less) for LA and Ventura counties.
confidence: Forecasters say models agree well through both the short and long term, with the main uncertainty being exactly how the swell and high tides line up midweek for coastal flooding.
